subject: Why AI design looks so generic
summary: Jordan argues that AI-built design becomes generic when agents fetch only text and then fill in visual details from priors. His core rule is to capture real screenshots and computed CSS, then build from those exact values and verify the result in a real browser.
nextAction: Probably archive or treat as FYI. If replying, send a short note that the capture-first framing is good and matches your own “ground truth beats priors” way of working.
preview: A long paid Substack post about why AI design looks generic and how to use real browser capture, CSS extraction, and layout gates to avoid average-looking output.
fullEmail:
From: Jordan Crawford <gtmontheedge+my-tools@substack.com>
To: r@rayamjad.com
Date: 2026-06-18 16:24:16 UTC
Subject: Why AI design looks so generic

A web fetch returns the words, not the pixels or the CSS. So Claude paints the rest from memory - that is the slop. The fix is one rule: capture, don't describe.

Jordan describes a workflow for using a real headless browser to capture screenshots plus computed CSS from strong reference pages, then building from those exact visual values instead of letting the model infer a generic pricing-page pattern. The post walks through a “Steal This Design” skill, including quick screenshots, deep CSS/token extraction, a decision page instead of a gallery, and a layout gate that catches overflow, broken images, clipped badges, buried recommendations, and weak mobile layouts.

The practical lesson: feed agents ground truth they could not have guessed, make the output commit to a recommendation, and verify the rendered page before shipping.

That is great. Glad you got to go and compare notes. Thanks for sharing the experience. That is an interesting insight that even in Anthropic engineering are pursing different workflows. Different types of work often require different paths.

I can't stand BMAD or rigid spec driven systems. either The process gets in the way of building. Sometimes I need to figure out what I want while I code in an interactive process. I can't write a detailed spec for something that is only 50% clear in my head sometimes. So different workflows for different situations.

Long winded comment on "Loops" and maybe an alternative explanation method below. In production scheduling there is this notion that you are operating on either a time and or a condition governing mechanism.

1. The hardest to pull off is fixed time and fixed condition (X is done exactly on this date). This is a traditional waterfall structure that often does not work.

2. Fixed time unfixed condition. I think this is what Agile / Scrum mainly does. Use a fixed time horizon and get done whatever prioritized. Then meet in X days and repeat, etc.

3. Fixed condition / unfixed time is another potential way to schedule. Work until a condition is achieved. Time continues until goal or condition is attained.

4. Unfixed time / unfixed condition is just zero planning and execution.

Loops are either a) fixed time (Chron job for example) and and then execute specified work or b) fixed condition (/goal) etc. and run until complete, etc.

Most are going to fall into this type of pattern? Or do you think about it differently? I am trying to simplify because just saying "loop" leaves me (and others I suspect) confused at times.

Art Smalley
